source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Eleven LLMs were run on a Wason 2-4-6 style rule-discovery game. They often test triples that fit their own guess instead of triples that could break it. This slows or blocks finding the hidden rule.
numbers: 11 model settings (Qwen3 8B/14B/32B, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, QwQ-32B, R1-distill-70B). Up to 45 turns. Task success from 6% to 78%. Test set 80 episodes per setting.
quote: Confirmation bias is a limitation of LLMs in hypothesis exploration
limits: Rules are integer-triple rules written by an LLM; success judged by an LLM judge. Metric is the incompatible:compatible test ratio (I:C), a proxy for disconfirmatory testing.
agent_relevance: S4 test choice: an agent that only verifies its own guess finds the hidden rule less often. Supports G3 and a code check that counts how many tests could fail.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Human baseline from Wason (1960) as restated by the authors: more disconfirmatory testing goes with finding the rule. LLM results show the same sign.
numbers: Wason 1960: 29 humans, 6/29 right on first announcement, 21/29 eventually right. I:C mean 1.79 for first-try correct vs 0.24 for first-try wrong. Second-try correct 0.50 vs 0.19.
limits: Human numbers are quoted from the LLM paper, not from Wason's original.
agent_relevance: Gives a human anchor for any I:C-style counter in our test step.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Across (model, variant) points, task success rises with I:C. Correlation is significant for both thinking and non-thinking models, stronger for thinking models. Same on the Blicket task.
numbers: Wason task: 80 episodes per point, significant positive correlations. Blicket task: 192 episodes per point, significant for both groups.
limits: Correlational across models, not causal; exact Wason rho not recovered from the PDF text.
agent_relevance: A falsification-rate counter could serve as a cheap process signal for good search.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Switching from non-thinking to thinking mode raises success but not consistently I:C. Gains from long reasoning are not mainly from less confirmation bias.
numbers: Qwen3-8B baseline: non-thinking 6% success, thinking 21%. Gemini-2.5-Pro thinking baseline 73% success, I:C 0.66. Qwen3-32B thinking baseline 41%, I:C 0.14.
limits: Table text in the PDF was garbled; only clean cells used.
agent_relevance: Longer thinking alone does not make the agent seek refutation; the scaffold must force it.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Think-in-Opposites prompt (test an instance opposite on one feature) improved success in all model settings and raised I:C in most. Dual-Goal (guess the rule and its complement) helped 8 of 11 settings.
numbers: Both interventions raise I:C in 18 of 22 cases. Qwen3-8B thinking: success 0.21 to 0.36, I:C 0.15 to 0.35 with TiO. Qwen3-32B thinking: 0.41 to 0.61, I:C 0.14 to 0.54. Average rule discovery 42% to 56% across prompting interventions. Gemini-2.5-Pro: 0.73 to 0.78.
quote: Prompting LLMs with such instruction consistently decreases confirmation bias in LLMs, improving rule discovery rates from 42% to 56%
limits: Significant for thinking models only; for non-thinking models results mixed (small gain TiO, small drop Dual-Goal). Dual-Goal needs a rule with a well-defined complement.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a prompt-level operator in S4: ask for the opposite test, or the complement hypothesis. Effect is large on reasoning models, weak on plain ones.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: The falsification habit can be trained in by supervised distillation of the Think-in-Opposites behavior, and it partly carries over to a new task (Blicket detector).
numbers: 72,000 training examples (1,600 episodes x 45 turns). Qwen3-8B baseline 0.21 success; same-model TiO distillation 0.35; 8B student from 32B TiO teacher 0.59. Qwen3-32B own TiO distillation 0.64 (TiO prompt teacher 0.61). Blicket: 32B base 0.57 to 0.77 after Wason distillation, below TiO prompt 0.86; 8B 0.32 to 0.34-0.38.
limits: Gain on Blicket is smaller than from prompting; only two task families. We do not train.
agent_relevance: The prompt version works; transfer across tasks is partial, so keep the operator in the scaffold for every task.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Blicket-detector variant (AND/OR/XOR rules, 4 or 8 objects): TiO helps thinking models, but not every model and not non-thinking ones.
numbers: 192 episodes. Qwen3-32B thinking 0.57 to 0.86 with TiO, I:C 0.54 to 1.31. Qwen3-32B non-thinking 0.64 to 0.56 (drop). R1-distill-70B 0.41 to 0.43. QwQ-32B 0.80 to 0.82.
limits: Single seed per cell as reported.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the opposite-test prompt is safe for every model; measure per model.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: FalsifyBench replaces numbers with WordNet categories so models cannot rely on a memorised 2-4-6. Games force a too-narrow first hypothesis, so only negative tests (outside the hypothesis) can show the rule is broader.
numbers: 12 LLMs, 100 games each (n=1,200 games), max 20 turns, 7 target categories. Best instruction-tuned model DeepSeek-V3.1 41%; others 33-35%. Reasoning models: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%. GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%.
limits: Oracle is also an LLM (accuracy 85-95%, kappa 0.34 to 0.98). Games built on H narrower than R, the case where negative testing is the only way.
agent_relevance: Shows the headroom: even the best 2026 model is at 75%. Usable as an external check for a falsification operator.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: Share of positive (confirming) tests predicts failure. Reasoning models test outside their hypothesis much more.
numbers: Spearman rho = -0.779 (p=0.003) between confirmation-bias ratio and success. Confirmation ratio: GPT-5-Mini 39.0%, GPT-5.2-Chat 27.3%, GPT-OSS-20B 24.2%; instruction-tuned 66-82%. Mixed-effects logistic regression n=1,200: coefficient -4.148 (OR 0.016); oracle error effect -0.123 (no credible effect).
limits: Observational; model identity is a random effect (SD 0.553). Prompt not varied.
agent_relevance: A per-game counter of confirming versus breaking tests is a strong predictor and costs nothing to compute in code.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: Applies Klayman and Ha: positive testing can falsify when H is broader than R, but not when H is narrower. The paper tags every turn with the set relation between H and R.
numbers: Conclusive falsification rate: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%, GPT-5-Nano 26.6%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%. Correlation with confirmation bias rho = -0.937 (p<0.001). H narrower than R in over 50% of turns for almost all models.
limits: Relation labels made by GPT-5-Mini, not human-checked at scale.
agent_relevance: Normative caveat for G3: 'prefer tests that can fail' depends on how H sits against the possible truth; a pure negative-test rule is not always best.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: Failure beyond confirmation bias: failed games have more hypotheses that only partly overlap or are disjoint from the target. Failed games also have more guesses and higher confirmation bias within the same model.
numbers: Partial-overlap turns, failed minus successful games: GPT-5.2-Chat +27.0 pp, GPT-OSS-120B +22.3 pp, GLM-5 +21.4 pp. Within-model confirmation: GPT-5.2-Chat 20% (won) vs 50% (lost); GPT-OSS-20B 17% vs 53%. Llama-4-Maverick 8.5 guesses per failed game vs 3.8 per won game.
limits: Descriptive analysis by LLM annotator.
agent_relevance: Test selection is not enough; hypothesis generation must also stay on a path. Pair S4 with a rule that limits blind guessing.

source: Huang, Jin, Li, Li, Candes, Leskovec (2025) Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications (POPPER)
finding: POPPER: LLM agents design falsification experiments for a free-text hypothesis; e-values are combined across tests to keep Type-I error under a set level. This is a working Popper loop inside an agent.
numbers: Type-I error target 0.1. Baselines exceed it: CodeGen(o1) 0.248, Self-Refine 0.117, some baselines 0.145 to 0.311 on single datasets (cell-to-method mapping partly garbled). POPPER at or under 0.1. 5 runs each. Six domains; DiscoveryBench, TargetVal-IL2, TargetVal-IFNG.
limits: Needs a data source and valid p-values; relies on strong coding LLMs (Claude Haiku 3.5 had high Type-I error).
agent_relevance: Template for S4 with a statistic: sub-hypothesis implied by H, test it, accumulate evidence with a rule that cannot be gamed by many tries.

source: Huang, Jin, Li, Li, Candes, Leskovec (2025) Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications (POPPER)
finding: Power and speed against human experts and baselines.
numbers: Among methods with Type-I control, POPPER has 66.5% more power than ReAct on DiscoveryBench and 3.17x Self-Refine on TargetVal-IL2. Nine biologists: no significant difference in Type-I error or power; POPPER 9.7x faster, 3.6x more code lines, 2.5x more tests.
limits: Human study is small (9 participants, 18 tasks); authors say no significant difference 'given the small sample size'.
agent_relevance: Evidence that an automated falsification loop reaches expert-level checking at lower cost.

source: Huang, Jin, Li, Li, Candes, Leskovec (2025) Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications (POPPER)
finding: Ablations and failure analysis show which parts of the falsification loop matter.
numbers: Removing the relevance checker raises Type-I error. Relevance checker vs 3 human raters on 90 proposals: Spearman 0.55 (p=5e-6); LLM called 85% strongly implied vs 77% by humans; Kendall W among humans 0.91. Failure causes: misinterpreted p-values 35.9%, weak experiment design 28.1%, test breaks implication 17.2%, wrong implementation 8.6%, hallucination 0.8%. Power rises with more allowed tests, Type-I stays controlled.
limits: Failure labels assigned by o1 then checked by humans.
agent_relevance: A check that each test truly follows from the hypothesis is needed; otherwise tests are irrelevant and results mislead.

source: Sinha, Goel, Kumaraguru, Geiping, Bethge, Prabhu (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? Evaluating Algorithmic Reasoning with Counterexample Creation (REFUTE)
finding: REFUTE tests the inverse skill: write an input that breaks a subtly wrong program. Models solve many of these problems from scratch but rarely find the counterexample.
numbers: 324 Codeforces samples (2024-2025). Best agent (o3-mini high with code execution) breaks under 9% of wrong solutions, though its rating implies it could solve up to about 48% of the problems from scratch. R1 similar.
quote: can create counterexamples for only < 9% of incorrect solutions in REFUTE
limits: Domain is competitive programming; validity checked by running code against a held-out correct solution.
agent_relevance: Falsifying is harder than producing: do not assume a model that can solve can also refute. Needs execution-based checks.

source: Sinha, Goel, Kumaraguru, Geiping, Bethge, Prabhu (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? Evaluating Algorithmic Reasoning with Counterexample Creation (REFUTE)
finding: Giving the correct solution does not fix the gap. Prompting for randomized brute-force search helps non-reasoning chat models a little and hurts reasoning models.
numbers: With the correct solution available, o3-mini breaks only 3% new submissions; with the random-search prompt it breaks 6% distinct new ones. 35% of RandSearch samples end with an invalid counterexample; 86% of those fail on wrong brute-force code, 14% on test validation.
limits: Few-shot examples used only for non-reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Tool-based search (generate many inputs, compare with a reference) can add refutations a model cannot reason out. Verify the reference code too.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing Experiments and Revising Rules with Natural Language and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: Online Bayesian experiment design with natural-language hypotheses (LLM proposes and revises, sequential Monte Carlo weighs). LLMs revise hypotheses well but propose experiments no better than a random generator.
numbers: Zendo: human accuracy 5.26/8 test scenes; ReAct-style LLM agent 4.60/8; best model 6.55/8. Fit to human accuracy R2: fuzzy online model 0.57, hard rules 0.10, batch 0.05, direct ReAct LLM 0.25. A hand-coded random experiment proposer performs about like the LLM proposer.
quote: do not consistently outperform random guessing when proposing experiments
limits: GPT-4 Turbo proposer; two domains (Zendo, ActiveACRE). The LLM was asked for experiments that support and falsify each hypothesis, then re-ranked by information gain.
agent_relevance: Let the LLM list candidate tests, but let code rank them (information gain). Reranking matters more than the LLM's own choice of experiment.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath, Hwu (2024) WILT: A Multi-Turn, Memorization-Robust Inductive Logic Benchmark for LLMs
finding: WILT (Wason Inductive Logic Test): hidden three-number boolean rule, up to 30 tests, one final guess. Strong single-turn models score low.
numbers: 50 rules. Accuracy: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50 (28%), o1-mini 13/50, o1-preview 12/50, chatgpt-4o-latest 11/50, GPT-4o 9/50, Gemma 2 9B 0/50. Sonnet also had 10/50 'approximately correct' extra.
limits: 2024 models; small N; rule must be equivalent to count as right.
agent_relevance: Baseline for how bad plain testing is; a cheap regression test for any falsification scaffold.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath, Hwu (2024) WILT: A Multi-Turn, Memorization-Robust Inductive Logic Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Error case study: o1-preview failed an easy rule (x >= y >= z) with 9 tests, five of them confirming 'all three equal' and none looking elsewhere. Test quality and deduction quality are separable skills.
numbers: Cross-model test swap: o1-mini is much better at deducing from other models' tests than from its own; Sonnet's results fell more than others when its stated reasoning was removed. Repeated tests per game: Deepseek-v2.5 9.78, Mistral Large 2.84, o1-preview 0.06.
limits: Qualitative plus a 2000-lambda hypothesis-space reduction estimate.
agent_relevance: Log repeated or non-informative tests in code and reject them. Separate 'propose test' and 'read result' steps.

source: Numberwang: LLMs Doing Autonomous Research (Alignment Forum pilot, 2024-25)
finding: Informal pilot (preregistered blog post): 11 LLMs on 10 hidden integer-list rules. Main failure beyond format errors was confirmation bias even when the prompt told them to falsify. Models also added epicycles (special cases) instead of dropping a hypothesis.
numbers: Mean 11% and median 10% of 10 rules found; 4 of 11 models got 0, 5 of 11 got 1; o1-preview 3, Claude 3.6 Sonnet 4. About 25% of runs failed on valid JSON (mostly smaller models). Authors' own 4-round human baseline was informal.
quote: models failed to consistently attempt to falsify their hypotheses
limits: Blog post, not peer reviewed; models are late-2024.
agent_relevance: Telling the model 'avoid confirmation bias' did not enforce it. The scaffold needs a code check, plus a limit on patching a hypothesis with special cases.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Wason selection task in LLMs: models reproduce the human pattern that realistic rules are easier than abstract ones; absolute accuracy low in both.
numbers: Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 show a realistic-rule advantage (z > 2.2, p < 0.03); PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2 marginal (p <= 0.08). Most human subjects at or below chance; slower humans above chance on realistic rules. Some models beat humans on nonsense rules.
limits: Forced choice of two cards, scored by log-probability; error patterns differ from humans in detail.
agent_relevance: Selection-task skill is content bound, so a falsification check should not depend on the model recognising a familiar story.

source: Seals, Shalin (2024) Evaluating the Deductive Competence of Large Language Models
finding: Wason selection task, social-rule content, ~7B models: social rules help somewhat but far less than in people.
numbers: Humans solve social-rule problems about 70% of the time (Griggs and Cox 1982); the LLMs about 30% (DC-PMI scoring); chance 1/6. Four ~7B models (Guanaco, MPT, BLOOM, Falcon). Presentation format changes gave no gains.
limits: Small open models; no fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: Old small-model evidence; modern models need retesting (see Lampinen).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Self-correction without outside feedback does not improve reasoning, and can make it worse. This is the self-critique case of failing to refute one's own answer.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5 75.9 to 74.7 after two rounds; GPT-4 95.5 to 89.0. CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 75.8 to 41.8; GPT-4 82.0 to 80.0. HotpotQA GPT-4 49.0 to 43.0. GPT-3.5 on GSM8K kept its first answer 74.7% of the time and changed correct to wrong more often than wrong to correct.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: 2023 models, three tasks; gains reported by others used oracle labels.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on the model checking itself; use external execution or counted checks.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist
finding: Google AI co-scientist uses a Reflection agent that checks each hypothesis (initial, full literature, and a deep verification that breaks the hypothesis into sub-assumptions and checks each for flaws), then an Elo tournament of debates.
numbers: 203 research goals: Elo of best hypotheses rises with more compute. 11 expert-rated goals: preference rank 2.36, novelty 3.64 and impact 3.09 out of 5. Ablation: giving Reflection search tools cut hallucinated 'novel' hypotheses; debate prompt in ranking reduced position bias. AML wet lab: Binimetinib, Pacritinib, Cerivastatin cut viability (Binimetinib IC50 as low as 2 nM); KIRA6 active in several lines.
limits: Expert-in-the-loop; subjective expert scores; Elo is a guide, not truth.
agent_relevance: A published agent loop where assumption-level refutation is a named stage. Matches our idea of decomposing a claim and attacking each part.

source: He et al. (2026) The Greatness of Science Cannot Be Planned: Agentic Auto-Research is Fuzz Testing
finding: Position paper with a simulated physics environment: agents that optimise a final score overfit and sample blindly; tracking dense intermediate evidence and keeping validation data protected helps find a hidden law and cuts false discoveries.
numbers: Only abstract and introduction read; no test numbers recorded.
limits: Simulated setting; claims are proposals to test.
agent_relevance: Keep a held-out check that the search loop cannot reuse; matches the worry about repeated testing in Popper-style loops.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: Positive test strategy is not the same as confirmation bias; when the true rule is broader than the guess, positive tests cannot reveal it, otherwise they can. This is the normative base used by FalsifyBench.
numbers: Not opened; described only as cited in FalsifyBench.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Use as the rule for when a negative test is needed.

source: King et al. (2004; 2009) Robot Scientist Adam and Eve: automated hypothesis generation and testing
finding: Older AI system: a robot that generates hypotheses about yeast gene function, runs the experiments itself and discards hypotheses the data contradict.
numbers: Not opened; no figures recorded.
limits: Not verified in this session.
agent_relevance: Earlier example of a closed falsification loop, with a physical lab.

source: Langley, Simon, Bradshaw, Zytkow (1987) Scientific Discovery: Computational Explorations of the Creative Process (BACON and relatives)
finding: Older AI systems (BACON etc.) rediscover laws from data by search and drop laws that fail to fit new data points.
numbers: Not opened; no figures recorded.
limits: Not verified in this session.
agent_relevance: Historical baseline; modern LLM loops add the language prior but need the same refute-and-drop rule.
